💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite being set in the past, WoW: Forever is an attempt to capture the spirit of the old game by injecting it with fresh quirks that challenge new and returning players alike to approach it differently than any other version of the MMO.
  • Recent findings suggest that blizzard has said that its goal is to "unsolve" the game as best it can so players don't settle into the same routines they're used to.
  • It's a lofty goal that can't be achieved without persistently fiddling with the knobs that encourage players to do one thing over another—which is the very thing that differentiates WoW: Forever from WoW Classic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite being set in the past, WoW: Forever is an attempt to capture the spirit of the old game by injecting it with fresh quirks that challenge new and returning players alike to approach it differently than any other version of the MMO. This is why familiar old dungeons can drop new loot, like an armor set that turns you into a snake.

Recent findings suggest that blizzard has said that its goal is to "unsolve" the game as best it can so players don't settle into the same routines they're used to. This is especially true for min-maxed strategies that threaten to suck the fun out of enjoying the game, or "the journey", as Blizzard likes to call it.

It's a lofty goal that can't be achieved without persistently fiddling with the knobs that encourage players to do one thing over another—which is the very thing that differentiates WoW: Forever from WoW Classic.

This week, Blizzard stepped in to fix a problem that was brewing in its 40-player MOBA-esque PvP mode Alterac Valley. Players were avoiding PvP altogether, turning it into a glorified reputation farm.

"We’ve seen that players in Alterac Valley were frequently completing the battleground without capturing the objectives, so we’ve made some adjustments to incentivize a focus on the objectives rather than rushing to kill the enemy faction’s general," community manager Kaivax wrote.

Industry observers note that the patch basically broke a popular 'zerg' strategy where one side rushed to end the match as fast as possible by beefing up the NPC defenders that stood in their way. Blizzard shifted some of the reputation and honor you'd normally get from killing the generals to the other objectives so players are encouraged to engage with the whole mode.

Recent findings suggest that but, as I've seen with changes like this in the past few weeks, many players are upset that they can't just spam it for the rewards, and that others have already reaped the benefits of the old strategy. There are people in Reddit threads doing the math to highlight how much efficiency has been lost (it doesn't seem like much) and questioning the point of doing Alterac Valley at all.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

While I sympathize with not wanting to do something that feels like a chore, it's a far worse problem to have an entire part of the game flattened into an AFK farm. Alterac Valley is supposed to feel like a large-scale war where you look at a major map and choose what objectives are worth fighting over as you try to weaken the enemy forces. The loot you get from maxing out your reputation with the associated factions is meant to be a reward for putting in the effort to learn what it takes to win.

The whole pitch for WoW: Forever is that it's not going to ditch everything with a upcoming expansion every few years. Numbers can be tweaked down the line if the reputation grind is too much of a slog, but the mode should be fun to play so it's not treated like a box to check off in your character's journey. An inert PvP mode ruins the spirit of the MMO far more than a slightly longer reputation grind does.

According to recent reports, I think this is a good example of a healthy change that shows Blizzard is committed to protecting core parts of the experience from becoming a treadmill that nobody enjoys. WoW: Forever's strengths are the ways it encourages you to participate in systems that aren't there to fill progression bars. As Harvey remarked in his WoW: Forever review, "Forever is proof that old-school MMO design deserves a second chance," and that requires taking a stance on what the game is and isn't meant to be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since.
  • Industry observers note that today, the Grammy Award–winning musician is one of the most celebrated classical violinists of his era.
  • That kinship was solidified over coupes of Champagne and hand-dived Orkney scallops, with the hotel celebrating Bell, a “Langham Luminary,” in its London ballroom packed with writers, artists, designers, and musicians.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since. “I don’t remember falling in love with music,” says Bell. “Music has just been my life. I used to string rubber bands on my dresser drawers and make pitches by pulling the drawers out. I was fascinated with strings. It’s the closest instrument to the human voice. And I find it the most expressive instrument.”.

Industry observers note that today, the Grammy Award–winning musician is one of the most celebrated classical violinists of his era. By 14, Bell was performing with the Philadelphia Orchestra, and would soon be touring the world. “I live in hotels 250 days a year,” says Bell of the nonstop schedule he has maintained since his teens. Specifically, Bell has been “staying at the Langham for decades now,” he says, referring to the regal central London hotel that first opened in 1865. “I chose it on my own because it was near one of my favorite halls in London, which is the Wigmore Hall. And now I stay with them whenever I’m traveling.”.

That kinship was solidified over coupes of Champagne and hand-dived Orkney scallops, with the hotel celebrating Bell, a “Langham Luminary,” in its London ballroom packed with writers, artists, designers, and musicians.

Attendees included actor Simon Callow, House of Dragon actor Emily Carey, former British culture minister Ed Vaizey, Saturday Night Live UK cast producer Susie Hall, stage and television actor Indira Varma, and Verity actor Ismael Cruz Córdova.

Held in partnership with Vanity Fair, the evening marked the latest iteration of the Langham’s Luminaries in Residence program. The event series is continuation of the hotel’s legacy that brings together a diverse, influential community—an evocative reminder of prominent guests from its storied past, including Charles Dickens, Winston Churchill, George Orwell, Oscar Wilde, and Mark Twain.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m not going to put my name in the same sentence as Toscanini or Mark Twain—who has stayed here, or Churchill, who has stayed here. But it’s cool to be part of the history,” says Bell. “So maybe someday, in a hundred years, there will be a violinist who might say that—that I stayed here. I don’t know, maybe that would mean something.”.

In a recent development, it certainly does mean something. Pierce Brosnan and his wife, Keely Shaye Brosnan, “have been huge fans of Joshua for many, many years,” Brosnan tells me. “Keely went to go see him…I don’t know how many years back. Unfortunately, due to the LA traffic, she got there late, five minutes late, and they wouldn’t let her into the concert. So tonight is one of those nights.”.

Bell, who performed mid-dinner with members of the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields—with a surprise appearance from his wife, soprano Larisa Martínez—brought about a collective catharsis.

According to recent reports, dazzling, fiery, and flamboyant, the experience of watching Bell up close is impossible to replicate. “I just think he’s incredibly soulful, and there’s something really elegant,” actor Russell Tovey tells me, before explaining how he actually discovered Bell via his Instagram algorithm.

For actor Lesley Manville, the event marked her introduction to Bell’s music. “I’m a bit embarrassed that he was not on my radar. But isn’t that nice to have a surprise like that?” says Manville. “Schubert’s String Quintet is one of my favorite pieces of music. It’s unbelievably beautiful. You think of a violin, you think of those strings. And it’s instant emotion. They just make you cry.”.

There is a great power in being able to access the emotions of others, as Bell does.

“I think it is the ultimate gift to be able to make people happy,” indicates Brosnan. “My job is being an entertainer—to take the words of great writing and try to transform it into something that is meaningful and memorable.”.

It has been revealed that speaking of entertaining, the week’s announcement that Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond was front of mind. “I wish him every joy and every success. He and I made a movie a number of years ago called Remember Me. I played his father. So I was very, very pleased and joyful for his nomination and now his success, and I believe he will be magnificent.”.

It has been revealed that and that creative full circle is exactly what the night was advocating. “Our own Luminaries in Residence program reflects our belief that meaningful hospitality creates genuine connection with extraordinary talents with one another, and with arts,” Bob van den Oord, CEO of Langham Hospitality Group, explained as he took the stage. “The Langham isn’t simply a place to stay, but a place to gather, exchange ideas, and indeed celebrate.”.

Someone Just Pointed Out A Potential Problem With The Avengers: Doomsday Trailer, And Now I Can't Unsee It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've watched the latest Avengers: Doomsday trailer more times than I'd care to admit, and like most Marvel fans, I've been busy trying to figure out how the Russo Brothers plan to bring all these characters together.
  • As Avengers: Doomsday approaches its 2026 movie release, Jason Pargin, best known for his John Dies at the End series of novels, took to Instagram Reels to point out something peculiar in the latest footage.
  • Sources indicate that pargin points out that all the battle sequence footage takes place in vast desert landscapes or voids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've watched the latest Avengers: Doomsday trailer more times than I'd care to admit, and like most Marvel fans, I've been busy trying to figure out how the Russo Brothers plan to bring all these characters together. But author and social media personality Jason Pargin just pointed out something about the upcoming Marvel movie that genuinely hadn't occurred to me. Now that he's pointed it out, I'm having a hard time looking past it.

As Avengers: Doomsday approaches its 2026 movie release, Jason Pargin, best known for his John Dies at the End series of novels, took to Instagram Reels to point out something peculiar in the latest footage. In the video, see below, Pargin raises an interesting question about how Marvel stages its superhero battles. Specifically, where the heck is everybody else?

A post shared by Jason Pargin (@jasonkpargin).

Sources indicate that pargin points out that all the battle sequence footage takes place in vast desert landscapes or voids. He then contrasts the footage with the trailer for 2012's The Avengers, which opens amid the destruction of New York City. People run through crowded streets. Cars are overturned. Buildings are damaged, and civilians scramble to escape whatever is coming. Before we even see our favorite superheroes assemble, we're reminded that ordinary people are in danger.

Sources indicate that if you think back to that first team-up, remember, Captain America directs police officers to evacuate civilians during the Battle of Latest York. There's also that terrific sequence where Steve Rogers saves people trapped inside a bank. Those moments gave the destruction a human cost.

When you go through the Marvel movies in order, there's less and less of that in the newer stuff. Watching Iron Man and Thor knock aliens around is entertaining enough, but seeing terrified Fresh Yorkers caught in the middle helps explain why Earth's Mightiest Heroes need to be there in the first place. Looking back at some of Marvel's more recent movies, I can see where Pargin is coming from.

Consider Avengers: Endgame. The climactic showdown against Thanos takes place at the destroyed Avengers compound, where hundreds of superheroes and their allies fight across a devastated battlefield. It's an incredible sequence, and I wouldn't change much about it. But virtually no ordinary civilians are caught in the fighting.

Then there's Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania, which moves its central conflict into the Quantum Realm. That movie does feature a population threatened by Kang's rule, so innocent lives are certainly at stake. Still, the setting creates a different feeling than watching superheroes defend a recognizable city filled with people going about their lives.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

I don't think this is a problem with every MCU movie, either. Spider-Man: No Way Home has Peter Parker desperately trying to save people on a bridge, and the most recent Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day certainly has human stakes like Ned and MJ always seemingly in peril. And then there's Black Panther: Wakanda Forever, which makes the consequences of its conflict painfully personal. Marvel clearly hasn't forgotten how to make its battles feel consequential.

Industry observers note that that's also why I'm hesitant to judge Doomsday too harshly based on one trailer. We have no idea how the actual movie will establish its stakes, and marketing departments understandably gravitate toward spectacular shots of superheroes fighting. The footage we've seen could represent only a fraction of what the Russos have planned. Still, Pargin's observation has me thinking about what made that original Avengers movie work so well. I can't unsee it.

Sources indicate that I love massive new superhero movies and their big-budget showdowns as much as anybody. I've been waiting years to see the X-Men and Avengers work together, and I'll absolutely be there opening weekend. When Captain America stood between a frightened civilian and an alien invasion, you understood exactly what he was fighting for. I think newer comic book movies could benefit from grounding some of that spectacle in the lives of the ordinary people these heroes are supposed to protect.

In a recent development, hopefully, when Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18, we'll get some of those human stakes alongside all the superhero action. If not, there's always the original Avengers, which is available to revisit with a Disney+ subscription.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's a upcoming survival game blowing up on Steam, and it's not for the faint of heart.

Casualties: Unknown introduced on November 9 and it's since racked up more than 5,600 user reviews, 98% of which are positive, making it one of the highest-rated fresh survival games to hit Steam in some time.

Industry observers note that before you jump in, you should be ready for what sounds like an incredibly punishing, visceral experience built around some very heavy, disturbing themes like drug use, depression, self-harm, and severe mental illness. I remember writing a similar PSA before recommending the 2024 horror gem Mouthwashing, and while I haven't yet gone hands-on with Casualties: Unknown, it definitely sounds like it's in the same wheelhouse thematically.

The game puts you in the shoes (paws?) of a bioengineered, animal-like humanoid whose sole purpose is corporate experimentation, a mission of retrieving lost cargo from a cave system running through a hostile alien world. I already have a profound fear of spelunking, but being forced to do so by an evil corporation with literally zero regard for your well-being is about the most horrific manifestation of that fear I can fathom.

Things are equally, or maybe even more grim, on the gameplay side of things. You platform your way down 11 layers of progressively more dangerous cave systems and fight to avoid losing consciousness. "You will have to bandage yourself, fight infected wounds, and stabilize blood loss before losing consciousness. Additionally, your mood can greatly affect your chances of survival, too much doom and gloom will make your life harder," says developer Orsoniks.

It sounds a little like the 2017 survival game Rain World, in which you play as a "slugcat" in a dangerous wasteland. Except Casualties: Unknown almost centers around a unique, very gross "simulated limb and cardiovascular system" that requires keeping tabs on things like blood flow and oxygenation, as well as targeted medical intervention. Casualties: Unknown also has more roguelike elements like procedurally generated environments, permadeath, and run resets.

Also similar to Rain World, according to pretty much every Steam review I read, is Casualties: Unknown's extreme difficulty. Orsoniks itself describes the game as "an unforgiving cave-exploration survival simulator" and "a hardcore survival simulation" where "injuries are unavoidable," so you can forget about that no-hit run right now. One reviewer claims it's even harder than the 2020 roguelike Noita, yet another notoriously unforgiving game.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

Another Steam user lists the number of ways they've died, including: "Sepsis, a pulmonary embolism, a fractured tibia, landmine to the body, spike trap from foot to collar bone, had my jaw ripped off, overdosing, falling from a great height, getting thrown into a ceiling by a jump-mine, depression, drinking bleach accidentally, radiation sickness, normal sickness, poisoning, drowning, hyper and hypothermia, exhaustion, tiredness, blood loss, starvation, thirst, psychotic break, and enemies.".

Industry observers note that again, not for the faint of heart. But if you're the type of video game enjoyer who finds increasing reward proportionate to the level of adversity overcome, Casualties: Unknown seems like quite the value. And with almost 100% positive reviews, it sounds like it's very much worth the pain it inflicts on you.

World of Warcraft: Forever's best newly introduced enchantment has been quietly changed, leaving some casters on the back foot

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (440 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As World of Warcraft: Forever players dived into the game, they promptly discovered a specific weapon enchant that took area of effect spells to a whole other level.
  • Sources indicate that the enchantment in question was Revelation - a new addition to the game included as part of the new trade good reputations.
  • So for example, let's say you're a druid casting the Hurricane spell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As World of Warcraft: Forever players dived into the game, they promptly discovered a specific weapon enchant that took area of effect spells to a whole other level. Sadly, with a sudden hotfix last night, this particular use case for the enchant has been removed.

Sources indicate that the enchantment in question was Revelation - a new addition to the game included as part of the new trade good reputations. What it does is simple: when you fail to deal a critical strike with a spell, the next spell hit is guaranteed to do so. What made this particularly powerful is that the buff also worked with continuous area of effect spells, meaning an early instance of the spell not crit-ing would result in the remaining damage hits all dealing critical damage.

So for example, let's say you're a druid casting the Hurricane spell. This is a channel spell with a total of 10 seconds of cast time. Every second, it deals damage. If the first instance of damage at the one second mark doesn't crit, the remaining nine instances of damage would all crit. This resulted in absurd amounts of damage, and made players of druids, warlocks, and mages very happy.

Sources indicate that while strong enchantments are often pricey, this was notably cheap, due to the low-cost of resources used to create it and the low requirements to learn it. As such, people were spending a handful of gold for an early game enchantment that was being actively used all the way into the end game.

Sources indicate that it was admittedly a tad too strong, and the effect triggered on AOE spells was almost certainly an unintended effect of the enchantment. Last night, the fun came to an end. Now, the effect is used up as intended in long-casted spells. So going back to the example given, if the first instance of damage on Hurricane doesn't crit, then the second one still will. However, this will use up the effect, and the third instance of damage will revert to regular ol' damage numbers. It also seems as though it Revelation can't trigger more than once during a single channeled spell.

It has been revealed that this is the latest in a string of ongoing quickfire bug fixes and game adjustments being made to World of Warcraft: Forever. The devs have been continuously updating the game in an attempt to curb certain gold farms, following the discovery of a particularly lucrative Blackmaw Hold gold exploit. The dev team has expressed some interesting ideas for the game longterm, including a desire to kill best-in-slot gear.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale.
  • Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving.
  • According to recent reports, the major retailers running sales are the usual ones: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales have essentially become a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already announced their prepares and started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this Black Friday sale a great one. Here's everything you need to know about the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

According to recent reports, the major retailers running sales are the usual ones: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Right now, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Amazon Black Friday: November 19.

Best Buy Black Friday: November 19.

Walmart Black Friday: November 23.

Target Black Friday: November 27.

It has been revealed that black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Sources indicate that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Industry observers note that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

It has been revealed that prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#154801. Why did Rockstar Games make empathy a key mechanic in GTA 6? "Because it's fun" says head of development Rob Nelson

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1509 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Why did Rockstar Games make empathy a key mechanic in GTA 6? "Because it's fun" says head of development Rob Nelson

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's been plenty of chatter about Grand Theft Auto 6's 'honour system', so to speak, implemented here via what the game calls your Criminal Profile.
  • Sources indicate that our own Dom just wrote that they prefer to turn its notifications off, for instance, in favour of fully soaking into the immersion.
  • Some of that is genuinely interesting - I'm dubious as to whether that's really what this system is doing, for a start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's been plenty of chatter about Grand Theft Auto 6's 'honour system', so to speak, implemented here via what the game calls your Criminal Profile.

Sources indicate that our own Dom just wrote that they prefer to turn its notifications off, for instance, in favour of fully soaking into the immersion. Personally I quite like the pop-ups - I find the act of figuring out systems and how they're manipulated almost as fun as the games they're a part of. And pop-ups or no, the fact that GTA 6 can arguably be portrayed as 'rewarding' empathy and 'discouraging' the series' famous rampages of mass violence has sparked a fair bit of debate.

Some of that is genuinely interesting - I'm dubious as to whether that's really what this system is doing, for a start. Is it incentivising and disincentivising certain in-game behaviour, or just putting a label on it? And then, actually: does the act of labelling "psycho" behaviour alone actually become a disincentivising factor in itself?

According to recent reports, either way, until now Rockstar hasn't mentioned a great deal about why, exactly, this system - seen by some as one that builds empathy into GTA's chaotic world - was implemented in the first place. But during an interview I had with Rob Nelson, Rockstar Games' head of development, just before GTA 6's launch earlier this month, a little more on that came to light.

A little context is necessary here: Nelson's response was actually following a question I had about the overall approach to design that Rockstar took, and how its wider themes and intentions came about. As a part of that, he turned to this system - and how, in a way, it exists here because of the work the studio simply didn't want to leave behind after Red Dead Redemption 2.

Nelson explained that this all began when the team was in the early phase of exploring what type of game GTA 6 would be, in 2015 and 2016, while much of the studio was still working full-tilt on RDR2 - a game which itself didn't release until late 2018. The team was looking to "build up the sophistication of the NPC population, and also allow for more player choice than we had [before], and more options in terms of the way you interact with the world beyond just violence," Nelson told me.

The idea would be that "it's still a world of violence - but you could threaten somebody by aiming a gun at them and just robbing them, and they have a chance to comply. So you don't have to beat them to death to get their money." Ideas that were "simple things" in principle, he mentioned, "but they create a lot more work in terms of development of the sophistication of the systems.".

Then, as systems were gradually implemented, it became a question of "trying to marry up what you're doing in the open world with who we're saying you are in the narrative - more than we had, I would say, previously, in Red Dead 2." It's here where the system now referred to as the Criminal Profile started to form.

The thinking turned to "the nature of 'honour', which wasn't always a part of it" with Red Dead Redemption 2, Nelson continued, "but became part of it as we were working on this story and finding that the 'redemption arc' didn't feel so good when it was foisted upon you - and feelings that we had playing Red Dead sort of early on." (Those feelings, primarily, were around getting you to invest in a gang led by Dutch Van der Linde, who was fundamentally unlikable from the off - or plain "crazy", as Nelson put it. The implementation of more player choices and agency was part of Rockstar's way to build investment in Arthur, even as he followed Dutch.).

Recent findings suggest that that meant moving the choices away from key story moments, where many games tend to put them. Instead, Rockstar built a system that ran alongside the story via smaller, moment-to-moment choices you might make. "We tried to take all of those off the main flow and make them optional. So again, they're a choice.".

Recent findings suggest that "Usually they involve some form of slight sacrifice or more effort on the part of the player," he added. The hope, then, was that you as a player would both "feel something", and ultimately also feel "you got the outcome that you deserved.".

That was the initial thinking behind this kind of system as a whole. Coming to GTA 6, it then combined with a wider desire to "evolve" Grand Theft Auto as both the team's storytelling and the available technology matured. "You're thinking about story and character set, but we're also thinking about what we want to do with GTA as a series, and how you want to evolve it," Nelson noted.

"I think as the resolution goes up, it sort of asks different new questions," he continued. "As the resolution goes up, you want the sophistication of the experience to go up, and obviously the sophistication of the mechanics. So it just naturally flowed that we give players choices to interact with the world beyond just violence, beyond just 'down the barrel of a gun', because it's fun.".

According to recent reports, "It's fun for some people like myself to just sort of role-play in the world, and be in the world, and restraint becomes something you hadn't thought about," he continued. That tied back into the more sophisticated NPCs and reactions the team were making.

Sources indicate that "If you think about the NPCs, even back to [GTA] 5, you would draw a weapon - first of all, they didn't react if you drew an invisible shotgun out of nowhere, or a rocket launcher," he mentioned. "They don't react unless you aim it, and then they flee in terror, and you're just sort of this demigod stomping through the world, you know? And that's fun, but for how long?

In a recent development, "The team then started thinking of ways to build a bit more sustained enjoyment from it. "What if you can't do that?" Nelson continued. What if, instead of whipping an RPG out of nowhere, "you have to call your car. You have to pop a car trunk and get it, and now I'm walking, and now people are noticing, but they're sort of sidling away, and it's more believable. And then they're still fleeing in terror, but then there's people who also have guns, and they're shooting at you, or you try to hold somebody up and they pull a gun, or they grab it, and then you have to deal with them.

According to recent reports, "And then, he continued, "you choose. You're trying to jack somebody off a motorcycle, and they pull a gun on you, and you have to blow their head off and it's like, 'You shouldn't have made me do that!' And so then it has more meaning, and it's more funny in a way when it's a little bit more pointed. And you can still go on those rampages and basically smash your Criminal Profile until it breaks and then you enter this irredeemable state, which basically claims 'I reject your criminal profile system! I don't want it.'".

In a recent development, that Irredeemable profile level, for what it's worth, was another element born of Red Dead Redemption 2. "We had that with Red Dead, where people would sort of have low honour, and then 'greet' their way back up to high honour. And so this was an attempt of sorts of [making something] for people that just want to go crazy and almost opt out of the system. They can opt out of it - and you can also turn off the notifications in the system.".

Industry observers note that it's notable, in fact, just how interlinked the thinking was with GTA 6 and Red Dead Redemption 2. As Nelson put it at one point: "There was maybe more emotional resonance in the story of RDR2 than we had had, certainly in a GTA before. So we liked that idea." What Rockstar did with GTA 6 was then in a way a natural next step. "We didn't necessarily come to GTA 6 going: 'We must have emotional resonance,' but all of those things combine. It's more that those systems and that element of player choice and agency, and the way that affected the narrative, was a hard thing to ignore and walk away from.".

According to recent reports, we'll have much more like this from our interview with Nelson very soon, so do look out for that on Eurogamer over the coming days. In the meantime, we've a handy guide explaining exactly how GTA 6's Criminal Profile system works and how to change, raise, or lower that profile if you're in need of a deep dive into how it all really works.

  • It has been revealed that according to royals author Russell Myers, who followed the couple on tour, the speech Kate gave at the awards was kept top secret.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that prince William and Kate Middleton’s visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony marked their first joint overseas tour in four years, and the couple used it as an opportunity to demonstrate their star power. Through their action-packed itinerary, which took them from Mumbai to New Delhi, the Prince and Princess of Wales have paved the way for a new style of royal tour.

From Kate unexpectedly presenting an award and delivering a speech at the star-studded Earthshot Prize event to her and William playing cricket and traveling around Mumbai in an electric rickshaw, there have been plenty of photo opportunities and headlines around the world about the environmental initiative William is so passionate about.

It has been revealed that according to royals author Russell Myers, who followed the couple on tour, the speech Kate gave at the awards was kept top secret. “None of us knew she was presenting an award on the night, or that she was going to speak. The auditorium was packed. There were about 5,000 people there. It’s been the biggest Earthshot yet, and you could see Catherine was nervous, but she delivered an absolutely brilliant speech. I’d say her best yet.

“It’s been wonderful for her to be here, supporting William, and you can see they’ve really had fun. Because of ongoing terror threats, there have been less walkabouts, but it’s been a very successful and varied tour, and I think, being shorter than most tours, it sets a newly introduced blueprint when it comes to royal tours for the couple in the future.”.

Prince William and Princess Kate arrive to attend the Earthshot Prize awards night at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

There are seemingly already looks for another royal tour, states Myers.

“William let slip that Australia is on the cards next, and if that’s the case, I imagine they will go as a family. They don’t want to be away from their children for too long, and what a way it would be to win support for the monarchy Down Under,” Myers says.

According to royals insiders, there had been some nervousness around the trip after the couple’s disastrous tour of the Caribbean in March 2022, when their visit was overshadowed by calls for the UK to apologize for slavery. Then some of their photo calls, including one that involved the couple riding in an open-top Land Rover, led to accusations of the royals appearing colonial and out of touch.

“I think there has been a slight nervousness about how this tour would be received, but the reception has been really good,” Myers says. “The fact that William and Catherine have included a visit to Newly introduced Delhi to see Prime Minister Modi is a clever move. While this is a private trip to promote Earthshot, the Foreign Office was keen for William to meet with the Indian prime minister, so they have packed that into the itinerary too.”.

In a recent development, the visit to India has come at a time when the royals are on something of a charm offensive following a difficult year for the royal family, from Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest to what one palace insider calls “the ongoing soap opera” with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has not been charged and has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.).

According to recent reports, william and Kate are keen to carve out their own initiatives and projects focusing on their major priorities, including the environment, children’s early years, and mental health. With the challenge of having Harry and Meghan carrying out their own engagements, the Prince and Princess of Wales have been careful to establish clear parameters that set them apart as working royals. In one telling moment while on an engagement in Mumbai, Kate was asked for an autograph. She politely declined, so as not to breach protocol, a clear contrast to the Duchess of Sussex, who has signed autographs in the past.

“Catherine was asked to sign an autograph, but she was right not to. It wasn’t a snub; it was just adhering to protocol. An autograph could be sold for money,” notes Dickie Arbiter, former press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II.

According to author Tom Bower, the royals are more relatable now than they were during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, who famously never gave a press interview. In recent weeks, Prince William has appeared as a guest on The Graham Norton Show (to promote Earthshot), and he’s revealed how he drinks his cider and his love of wild swimming as part of his guest-editing stint for a recent concern of Country Life magazine.

It has been revealed that “The royals are more relatable, perhaps, than they ever have been, but they are not celebrities. There’s a danger of being too relatable, too much ‘one of the people,’ which means they can lose some of their mystery,” Bower claims.

“William will have been advised to do TV appearances and take on media opportunities to bolster his public image. Of course, it’s charming to hear these nuggets and see this side of the prince, but I do think there’s a need to see and hear more from William about his broader plans. Over the years, Charles has made huge efforts to appeal to all cultural aspects of society. I’m not sure William has done that. He’s got to find a way of connecting with everyone, not just the younger generation,” Bower adds.

The Earthshot Prize awards have been a powerful way of demonstrating that William doesn’t just talk the talk; he is insisting on action.

It has been revealed that “The Earthshot is a master class in what needs to be done,” concludes Arbiter. “He’s pushing for environmental concerns and climate change, and he’s getting people to do something about it. The fact that he is so well supported, and by so many high-profile people, indicates his pulling power and influence.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft-owned developer platform Github stepped in it earlier today when it posted a message on X celebrating the success of AnyPS5, an open source project that aims to let users port PS5 executables to PC, and then linked that success directly to efforts to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC.
  • "GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on Github," the message stated (via Kotaku).
  • According to recent reports, "The repo AnyPS5 has passed 58K stars since its August launch, rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft-owned developer platform Github stepped in it earlier today when it posted a message on X celebrating the success of AnyPS5, an open source project that aims to let users port PS5 executables to PC, and then linked that success directly to efforts to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC. The message was deleted shortly after it was posted, but not before it was widely noticed and called out for being a very bad idea.

"GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on Github," the message stated (via Kotaku).

According to recent reports, "The repo AnyPS5 has passed 58K stars since its August launch, rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line? Share your take. Happy GTA VImas!".

Lest there be any misunderstanding, a video that accompanied the post made the GTA 6 connection explicit: "The project rewrites a game's executable so Windows and Linux can run it directly. Performance seems to be the main problem for users wanting to run GTA 6, with one contributor telling the project's community to 'lock in and get your agents to help' if they need to.".

And here's the accompanying video from @github's GTA6 tweet https://t.co/crU9cpOWcsNovember 26, 2026.

Sources indicate that the question of whether or not this sort of thing crosses a legal line has, predictably, sparked debate among those who think they have a clear understanding of the answer. What caught most by surprise, though, is that Github—which is owned by Microsoft—would put forth the question in the first place, implicitly suggesting that it might not. GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive has been pretty aggressive with its efforts to keep recompiled versions of GTA 6 from landing on PC, and I can't imagine it would too thrilled with Github—which, I must emphasize, is owned by Microsoft—telling the world that it might actually be okay to go ahead and vibe-code it up.

That point wasn't missed by redditors, one of whom described it as Github "openly taunting Sony and Rockstar." Even the AnyPS5 subreddit seemed baffled: Redditor superkickstart asked, "Do they have AI running their socials? Lol".

Sources indicate that there's also a little bit of irony in the fact that, until earlier this week, the leading effort to get GTA 6 running on PC was based on an Xbox build of the game posted by GTA 6 leaker Cyberleeks. Beyond that, there are also some very obvious questions about how Github (owned by Microsoft) would react to AI-powered ports of, say, other software:.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Industry observers note that the whole thing is weird, really, because it seems like such an obviously bad idea. The only explanation I can come up with is that a social media manager either didn't think about it, didn't understand it (which would be weird in itself for someone doing social media posts for Github), or just had a massive ol' brain fart. Whatever the reason, I imagine someone got a good old-fashioned talking-to about it.

I've reached out to Github and Take-Two for comment and will patch if I receive a reply.

This is one of those rare opportunities that don't come often in the consumer tech space: Right now, you can get a 65-inch OLED TV from Samsung for $899.99 (originally $2,099.99) from Best Buy during its Black Friday sale. This 2026 TV is considered an "entry-level" OLED, but it's still an incredible value for the money and the lowest price it has ever had.

If you've never owned an OLED before, there are some things you need to know to make sure it's a good fit for you. Perhaps most important is that they don't get as bright as QLEDs or LED TVs. Since this is an entry-level OLED, it likewise won't reach as high brightness as more premium OLEDs. This makes it less suitable for viewing in very bright rooms. There is also no Dolby Vision support (though there is support for HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG). But that is where the cons end.

The S84H offers the near-perfect black levels you can expect from any OLED TV, making the contrast look incredible. The pixel-level dimming and viewing angles are also on par with other high-end OLEDs, and this TV also offers great features for gamers, including 4K support at 120Hz across all of its HDMI 2.1 ports, a variable refresh rate, and auto low latency mode.

Industry observers note that OLED TVs are not normally priced under $1,000, especially newer models like this one. It's an incredible value for the money. The last time a deal like this popped up was in February, and before that, last Christmas, but for the 2025 version of this TV. There's a chill in the air and a snowman (plastic) at the end of the street, meaning winter is firmly upon us. So what better way to make it way through the long dark nights than a spot of festmas gaming. And hark, just in the nick of time, PlayStation Plus' monthly games for December have been revealed, with some skating, spooking, and dragon baubles.

Not the most festive bunch, then, but some decent stuff all the same. Amnesia: The Bunker is a real winner if you like it spooky (and The Bunker is very spooky), setting players loose in a labyrinthine underground WW1 bunker where something awful prowls. It's a "truly unsettling adventure" as we wrote in our Amnesia: The Bunker review.

As for the other two, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3+4 is well worth your time, taking the beloved early 2000s skating games and giving them a successful modern-day makeover. We called it a "properly glorious collection of two classic games" in our Pro Skater 3+4 review. As for Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2, the critical consensus seems to suggest it is 'okay'.

For more information on PlayStation Plus, you can check out our guide to PS Plus and all the available games here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at this point on Marshals, I never use Cal’s full name, Pete Calvin. His nickname is used far more than his full name, and now, Cal’s putting in the work to make sure his team has nicknames like him. For example, as Season 2 of Marshals has been airing on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve noticed Cal calling Kayce Coyote a lot. So, with all this in mind, I asked Logan Marshall-Green, who plays Cal, what’s up with the nicknames, and specifically Kayce’s.

It has been revealed that back when Yellowstone was on, there was a lot of drama involving wolves and Kayce. So, I was a bit surprised when Cal started calling him Coyote (pronounced “ky-oat” instead of “ky-oh-tee”). However, it felt fitting for the Dutton family member. When I asked Marshall-Green about it, he told me it was an crucial thing that he and Luke Grimes wanted Cal to use with Kayce, too, and it all ties back to their military history:.

In a recent development, that was something Luke and I both were talking about being SEALs. You don't call people by their first names; you just don't. And so, also with the team, it's been crucial to try to find nicknames. So Luke was very adamant about finding a nickname for him that I could use. That was something that [creator Spencer Hudnut] came up with. I think it's like kind of a play on Coyote. I'm not sure if I gave him that name or if somebody else gave him Coyote and we just started calling him Coyote because of other people.

Industry observers note that so, the backstory behind the nickname is unknown, at least to Logan Marshall-Green. However, it is something that’s important to Cal and Kayce’s shared history. If I had to guess, Kayce got the nickname while they were both SEALs, and it’s just stuck. I personally hope Cal is the one responsible for it, and maybe someday that can be addressed in the show.

It has been revealed that while we wait for that backstory, Marshall-Green is putting in the work to get the rest of his team nicknames. In the show, we’ve heard Ash Santos’ Andrea referred to as Dre on multiple occasions, and that was a creation of the Cal actor. He personally went to Santos and Spencer Hudnut to ask them about it. He’s also trying to get nicknames for Tatanka Means’ Miles and Arielle Kebbel’s Belle to stick. Explaining all of that, he mentioned:.

According to recent reports, but you know, like Dre is something I approached Spencer and Ash about because I thought that would be a perfect name for Cal to call [her], because that's who he hired first for the team. And we're still trying to work – you know, there's Dust Cloud for Miles’, for Tatanka’s character. And I came up with a really good – I thought it was a really good nickname for Belle, but Ariel didn't love it. So yeah.

Recent findings suggest that so, we have Dre and Coyote. We have Dust Cloud too. However, Belle still does not have a nickname because it sounds like Kebbel vetoed it. Knowing Cal and Belle’s relationship, that feels hilariously fitting. However, I do hope that someday she can get a nickname too.

In a recent development, now, to see this team (and their nicknames) in action, you can catch latest episodes of Marshals on CBS every Sunday. You can also stream them the day after with a Paramount+ subscription.

#154793. EA is resurrecting a dead commentator with AI for EA Sports FC 27, years after his last appearance in a FIFA game

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (540 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

EA is resurrecting a dead commentator with AI for EA Sports FC 27, years after his last appearance in a FIFA game

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • EA Sports FC 27 is using gen-AI to digitally recreate the voice of veteran football commentator John Motson - the FIFA video game series' first ever real-world announcer who died in 2023.
  • John Motson commentated on hundreds of football games over the course of five different decades, starting in the 1970s.
  • But EA's now decided to digitally resurrect Motson - or, at least, his incredibly recognisable voice - with permission from his family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EA Sports FC 27 is using gen-AI to digitally recreate the voice of veteran football commentator John Motson - the FIFA video game series' first ever real-world announcer who died in 2023.

John Motson commentated on hundreds of football games over the course of five different decades, starting in the 1970s. The English commentator then became the mainstay voice of EA's dominant football simulation series, beginning with FIFA 96 all the way up until FIFA 2005, when the publisher decided to go in a different direction.

But EA's now decided to digitally resurrect Motson - or, at least, his incredibly recognisable voice - with permission from his family. An revision with Motson's voice will go live on 26th November. "There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," senior game designer director Mat Prior remarked in a statement given to the BBC earlier today.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back," Prior added, explaining that Motson's posthumous role in the game is being handled with a mixture of previously recorded voice lines and AI. EA supposedly went down the AI route since it doesn't have recordings of Motson commentating over newer, more fresh faced footballers.

It has been revealed that fred Motson remarked it "means an awful lot" to hear his dad's voice in the game again, and he reckons his dad was "always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects," even if he wasn't the most technologically savvy person. EA said it had paid the family for the rights to use Motson's voice and likeness.

Recent findings suggest that save Our Voices Now founder Peter Caulfield - who campaigns for the government to regulate the use of generative AI voice cloning tech - told the BBC he wasn't comfortable with the project. "In life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed," he noted. "Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either." He doesn't have a problem with actors consenting to AI voice replication while they're still alive, however.

A Japanese acting union recently fought back against this very same practice by proposing fresh guidelines that would stop the replication of dead actors' voices without their permission.

Recent findings suggest that generative AI has been widely controversial in the games industry for other reasons, too. In recent months, there's been a huge impact on smaller game developers who are worried that their games could be cloned by AI copycats and some who have had to delay their release dates because of Steam's growing approvals backlog.

"The Grounds comes across as a frippery, Ultimate Team rumbles ever on, but FC 27 brings meaningful changes to the fluidity and speed of play. Given that its practical football-game monopoly is more or less unchallenged, EA could do a lot less than this," Josh Wise wrote in Eurogamer's EA Sports FC 27 review.

#154789. Tech Report: This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2179 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vanityfair ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before.
  • In a recent development, on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades.
  • The twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unpredictable; when I went there this summer for lunch with a movie producer, we spotted a powerful name-brand media executive, an architectural bigwig who designs the homes of billionaires, and a two-time Academy Award–winning actor. A few nights later, I sat near Walter Isaacson, who’s a regular. And don’t just take it from Elon Musk’s biographer. Matthew Schneier, the chief restaurant critic at New York magazine, recently named Borgo the city’s best all-around restaurant.

In a recent development, on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

The twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

After launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had reveals recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.

As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

It has been revealed that “I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”.

Sources indicate that the studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They showed figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

The studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

In a recent development, “It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” says Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”.

Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

“I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”.

He told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

“What are the processes? Like you remarked, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”.

It has been revealed that diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.

“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

In a recent development, tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some new development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

In a recent development, A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few shows. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

“I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”.

Sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

Sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”.

As a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

“I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he remarked. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”.

Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

“I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”.

The show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

Industry observers note that the showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he noted. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

“I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew mentioned, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy says. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”.

It has been revealed that like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy claims, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.

And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

In a recent development, “I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he said. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brother of Hayden Panettiere’s on-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, is sharing an update on how he is doing following her tragic death in August.

“I spent almost eight to 10 weeks up in Greenville [South Carolina] around him,” Zach Hickerson said in an interview with TMZ published on Friday, November 27. “One word that comes to mind is just distraught, heartbroken, confused. I know that there’s still a certain level of shock and surrealness to him of that. There’s just no resolve to this. This isn’t, like, a legal thing. This isn’t a breakup thing. … It’s a definitive thing, and there’s no fixing [it]. There’s no resolve.”.

“He’s, one, navigating the loss [and] two … trying to look ahead at the next chapter of his life or the rest of his life. Like, what now?” Zach, 39, continued. “Given all that’s happened, given the reputation, I just know that he’s carrying a lot. Rightfully so, to an extent.”.

Panettiere was pronounced dead at the scene after authorities responded to a 911 call at an Airbnb in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16. The Heroes actress was staying at the residence with Brian, 37. Zach was also present.

It has been revealed that “I know that he’s heartbroken,” Zach shared on Friday. “I’ve tried to be there as much as I can for him. About three or four weeks ago, I realized that, man, I was probably trying to carry a little bit too much for everyone else and had not really dealt with the grief and loss myself. So I’ve taken the last two to three weeks to really kind of be on my own, so it’s hard for me to say exactly this moment in time how he’s doing. But what I witnessed was sheer distraught and despair.”.

In another clip from the TMZ interview published on Wednesday, November 25, Zach described discovering the Nashville star unresponsive inside the Airbnb.

“I didn’t think it was abnormal that she was [sitting], kind of, Indian-style and laid over,” he recalled. “Her hair was longer, so it was covering. I just assumed that she would pop up and be like, ‘Zachary, what are we doing today?’”.

“[Brian] took his hand and went, ‘Hayden,’ and when she didn’t immediately respond or make a noise or react, I stood up and moved to the side,” Zach continued. “Brian … pulled her onto his chest, and when he did, I had a clear view of her face, [which] was pale, lips were purple. I immediately knew something was incredibly wrong.”.

In a recent development, “We did CPR for, gosh I don’t even know how long it was. I just did it until the EMS and the cops and the fire and whomever else came in,” he said. “I was like, ‘Oh my God, thank God, they’re here.’ Brian and I got up, got out of the way.”.

Panettiere’s cause of death was the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. It was ruled an accident.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Action game maestro Hideki Kamiya really wants to make a latest Castlevania game with publisher Konami.

The long-time developer best known for his work in the director's chair on a host of beloved games - Bayonetta, Resident Evil 2, Okami, Devil May Cry and The Wonderful 101 included - recently published a latest video to his personal YouTube account. While the video was first recorded last year, it does give us some hints on what Kamiya is interested in making after his in-development Okami sequel wraps up.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the most noteworthy tidbit came from Kamiya advocating to make a new game in Konami's vampiric action-adventure series. "We'll definitely make Castlevania. If you let us work on it, we can make something truly insane, so just contact us and we'll be at your service," Kamiya noted. (Thanks, Automaton!).

Industry observers note that kamiya presumably has his hands full with Capcom's Okami 2, which is currently in production at the director's newfound independent studio Clovers. Needless to say, any potential Kamiya-led Castlevania game will likely need to wait in a coffin for a while more.

Recent findings suggest that in the meantime, it's not like Castlevania has remained dormant and defanged. Earlier this year, Konami promised that "numerous new products around Castlevania" are in the pipeline. While new games weren't explicitly confirmed, it's safe to assume Konami would be interested in hearing pitches from outside devs. Kamiya can stay hopeful knowing that Evil Empire just dropped another gorgeous, aggressive action-platformer in the series.

Industry observers note that "Like Rose herself, the game is earnest, intelligent, and capable of brilliance. But, mimicking its protagonist, it is also awkward, and unable to fully come to terms with its own unique identity in the shadow of its over-bearing legacy," Dom wrote in Eurogamer's Castlevania: Belmont's Curse review. "By no means is Belmont's Curse a bad game, I just think Evil Empire sunk its teeth a bit too deep into something it wasn't quite ready to consume.".

This isn't the first time Kamiya has publicly expressed interest in reviving older games, either. He recently said he's "100% serious" about bringing back Scalebound, his cancelled Xbox One exclusive.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that based on what we've seen of the Ork and Adeptus Mechanicus campaigns, that means partway through you'll be presented with a choice between two Commanders who have opposed goals and the one you pick will lead to missions with different objectives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The original Dawn of War's Winter Assault expansion added campaigns that let you play two factions at once, with different final missions based on which one you triumphed with. Dawn of War 2's campaign was even more player-led, with distress calls that had different outcomes based on what you prioritized and, in the Chaos Rising expansion, a morality mechanic with Corruption and Redemption points. It even chose a different character to be a traitor based on who gained the most Corruption by the story's end.

Industry observers note that I asked John French, Dawn of War 4's writer and a Warhammer novelist, whether Dawn of War 4 would follow this noble tradition by having player decisions alter the plot. "The player's decisions very much change the perspectives that they'll experience the game from," he replied. "So, depending on which heroes from each faction they choose, they'll have a very different experience of the game, in that they'll see different parts of the story and sometimes different views on the same events.".

Sources indicate that based on what we've seen of the Ork and Adeptus Mechanicus campaigns, that means partway through you'll be presented with a choice between two Commanders who have opposed goals and the one you pick will lead to missions with different objectives. Ork Beastboss Guzcutta is trying to unite his clan, the Snakebites, while his rival warboss, Gorgutz, is an off-world interloper trying to rebuild his damaged invasion force.

"With characters like Gorgutz and Guzcutta," French explained, "it can be as simple as one of them wants to do it the traditional, brutal ork way, and one of them wants to do it in a brutal but cunning way, so you have missions that focus on getting lots of shiny kit in one, while the other tries to get as many orks to follow them as possible.

"In a more complex narrative, like the Adeptus Mechanicus campaign, Potentia-Delta-9's main drive is the quest for knowledge, and she is on a very different path from Skitarii Marshal Sek-Ix-23, who is very much about enforcing the orthodoxy. The story for both overlaps, but which character you choose and what decisions you make with them lead down different experiences of an overlapping story.".

According to recent reports, writing an RTS isn't all about plotting out the campaign missions. The Dawn of War games are legendary for their unit barks, like the saber-rattling Lord Commissar who shouts, from the top of an armored Chimera transport, "Drive me closer, I want to hit them with my sword!" Getting across so much personality in a short space is a real skill.

Industry observers note that "You can do an awful lot with just a couple of words like 'More dakka!'," French noted, "that tells you a huge amount about the orks on its own. Even with factions like the necrons, the way that the lower ranks respond to the higher ones with just 'Obedience,' one word, tells how their faction works.".

According to recent reports, part of the appeal of Warhammer is the berserk variety of its armies, each with its own highly thematic identity. You walk into a shop and see the stoic space marines alongside spiky Chaos daemons and units of Astra Militarum who look like they stepped out of a trench in World War I before being given laser rifles.

"Dawn of War 4 is deeply Warhammer in that way because it's got all of these different textures of factions and characters next to each other," French said. "You have orks, and they are absolutely fixated on smashing everything they can in the pursuit of trying to have an even bigger fight. Then you've got the Adeptus Mechanicus, who revere machines as holy and worship the machine as god with complete sincerity and total conviction. Those two things literally exist side by side, along with alien races who have made themselves immortal by creating metal bodies with hyper advanced technology. And all of these different types of character come into conflict on one planet cut off in a sea of night—that's very Warhammer.".

Industry observers note that dawn of War 4 is due out on December 3 and will be available on Steam. Owners of the Commander Edition will get advance access and can play from November 30.

According to recent reports, jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. A former music journalist who interviewed everyone from Giorgio Moroder to Trent Reznor, Jody also co-hosted Australia's first radio show about videogames, Zed Games. He's written for Rock Paper Shotgun, The Major Glitch, GamesRadar, Zam, Glixel, Five Out of Ten Magazine, and Playboy.com, whose cheques with the bunny logo made for fun conversations at the bank. Jody's first article for PC Gamer was about the audio of Alien Isolation, published in 2015. Jody edited PC Gamer Indie from 2017 to 2018, and he eventually lived up to his promise to play every Warhammer videogame.
